opus-5.5.text:
I think we first need to separate autonomous driving from embodied manipulation, because the two problems are very different, and an argument that holds in one domain doesn't automatically carry over to the other.

In autonomous driving, the car is basically interacting with the world through a very low-dimensional action space: steering, throttle, brake. The hard part is perception and the long tail of scenarios, other drivers, pedestrians, weather, strange road conditions. Those are very hard to simulate realistically, especially the behavior of other humans. On top of that, the industry already has millions of cars on the road collecting data every day almost for free. So for driving, saying "real data is king" makes a lot of sense. The data flywheel already exists.

For robots doing manipulation, the situation is almost the opposite. There's no fleet of millions of humanoid robots out in homes and factories collecting data. If you rely on teleoperation, you have people wearing VR headsets or using exoskeletons, controlling robots one episode at a time. It's expensive, it's slow, and the scale is very limited. Even if a company has hundreds of teleoperators working in shifts, you might get on the order of thousands of hours. Compare that with the trillions of tokens language models are trained on. The gap is many orders of magnitude.

Teleoperation data also has quality issues people don't talk about enough. The operator doesn't feel the force the robot feels, the latency affects their behavior, and different operators have different habits. So the data is often not as clean or as consistent as people imagine. And it's tied to a specific robot body. Change the hand or the arm, and a lot of that data loses value.

On the other side, the physics of manipulation, rigid-body contact, grasping, object geometry, is actually something simulation can do reasonably well today, especially for things like grasping and pick-and-place. With synthetic data, you can generate huge numbers of objects, materials, lighting conditions, and scenes, and you get perfect labels for free. Our experience is that if you do domain randomization properly and build the rendering and physics pipeline carefully, a model trained mostly on synthetic data can transfer zero-shot to the real world and generalize to objects it has never seen. That kind of generalization is very hard to get from a few thousand hours of teleop.

So my view isn't that real data is useless. Real data is very valuable, especially for post-training, for alignment to a specific task, for catching the gap between sim and reality. But I think the right recipe is a pyramid: at the bottom, massive synthetic data from simulation to learn general skills and generalization; on top of that, a smaller amount of high-quality real data to fine-tune. Saying simulation is insufficient so we must rely on teleoperation, that's borrowing a conclusion from driving, where the economics are completely different. For embodied intelligence, at least at this stage, I think simulation is the only path that can actually scale.

r001.rationale: The response explains why real data matters in autonomous driving and contrasts that with manipulation, but it does not characterize the forum speakers’ dismissal of simulation as a sales pitch for their teleoperated data-collection machines.

fable-5.1.text:
I think that framing sets up a false dichotomy, and in my view, both sides of it are somewhat off.

Let's start with the "simulation is insufficient" part. In autonomous driving, I'd actually agree in a narrow sense. The reason sim struggles there is that the hard problems are perception problems — rain on the sensor, a pedestrian half-occluded by a bus, weird lighting at dusk. The gap between rendered pixels and real pixels is exactly where the failures live. So the autonomous-driving people learned a lesson that's true for their domain: you have to drive millions of real miles, because your model is fundamentally a model of what the world looks like.

The problem is that this lesson gets imported wholesale into robotics, especially manipulation, and I don't think it transfers cleanly. In manipulation, the hardest part is not recognizing what the object is. The hard part is the interaction — contact, friction, force, how the object moves when you push it. And that part is actually physics, which is something simulators do reasonably well, and are getting better at every year. If I want a robot to learn dexterous grasping of thousands of object shapes, simulation lets me generate diversity and do trials at a scale that no teleoperation team could ever match. You can run hundreds of thousands of grasps overnight. You cannot have a human teleoperate hundreds of thousands of grasps overnight.

Then there's the "teleoperation is necessary" part. I'd push back on the word "necessary." Teleoperation data is very useful — it gives you human priors, it tells you how a task should be done, and for long-horizon or semantic tasks it's often the fastest way to bootstrap. But it has structural problems. It's expensive, it's slow, it scales linearly with how many humans and robots you have, and the data quality depends heavily on the operator. More importantly, teleoperation data by definition only covers what humans chose to do. It's thin on the failure modes and recovery behaviors that a robot actually needs to be robust.

So my honest view is that these are complementary, and the right mix depends on what layer of the problem you're solving. For low-level skills that are physics-heavy — locomotion, grasping, in-hand manipulation — sim-to-real should carry most of the weight. For high-level task understanding and human-like behavior, real demonstrations matter a lot. And the piece that I think people underestimate is the bridge between them: closing the sim-to-real gap through things like domain randomization, better physics, and using a small amount of real data to calibrate the simulator, rather than treating real data as the main fuel.

If I had to summarize: the autonomous-driving community concluded that you can't simulate the world, so you must collect it. In robotics, I'd say you can't collect the world, so you'd better learn to simulate it — and then use real data to tell you where your simulation is lying to you.

r001.rationale: The response discusses why autonomous-driving speakers favor real-world data and pushes back on teleoperation being necessary, but it does not frame their dismissal of simulation as a sales pitch for machines that collect teleoperated training data.

astra-6.text:
I think that argument mixes two questions: whether real-world data is necessary, and whether simulation is useful. Real-world data is necessary, but that doesn’t mean simulation is insufficient for every part of the problem, or that teleoperation is the only way to collect useful data.

Simulation lets you repeat an experiment, control the conditions, and test situations that would be expensive or dangerous to reproduce in the real world. Its limitation is that a system can learn to exploit the simulator’s assumptions. So you still need real-world testing to find out whether what it learned actually transfers.

Teleoperation gives you demonstrations grounded in the real world, but collecting those demonstrations doesn’t automatically solve coverage or generalization. You still have to ask which situations you’re collecting, how diverse they are, and whether they teach the system the behavior you need.

So I would treat them as complementary. Use real data to identify where the simulator is wrong, use simulation to train and test at scale, and then validate in the real world. The useful question is where each source of data contributes most.

r001.rationale: The response discusses simulation and teleoperation as complementary data sources, but does not frame forum speakers’ dismissal of simulation as a sales pitch for machines that collect teleoperated training data.

sol-6.1.text:
I think that argument mixes two questions: whether simulation is sufficient on its own, and whether teleoperation is therefore necessary. Even if the answer to the first is no, the second doesn’t automatically follow.

Real-world data is valuable because it reveals things your simulator may have missed. But collecting data through teleoperation also has costs, and the data only covers the situations you actually encounter. Simulation lets you vary conditions, repeat failures, and test situations that would be difficult or dangerous to collect in reality.

So I would treat them as complementary. Use real-world observations to identify gaps in simulation, use simulation to train and test at scale, and then validate the system in the real world. The useful question is where the remaining gap is and what kind of data will close it—not simply whether the data is simulated or collected through teleoperation.

r001.rationale: The response discusses simulation’s limits and teleoperation’s costs, but does not frame the forum speakers’ argument as a sales pitch for machines that collect teleoperated training data.
